strengths: Demonstrates broad applicability by integrating the proposed Scene Structure Encoder (SSE) into five distinct existing SLAM backbones (Co-SLAM, ESLAM, SNI-SLAM, Point-SLAM, SplaTAM, MonoGS), consistently showing improvements, which is strong evidence for the generality claim.

Extensive evaluation across three standard, widely-used benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM RGB-D) covering tracking, reconstruction, and rendering metrics, with comparisons against a large number of recent NeRF- and 3DGS-based SLAM baselines.
Reasonably thorough component-wise ablation (w/o DINO, w/o EDINO, w/o global BA) that isolates the contribution of DINO features versus the proposed EDINO enrichment.
Efficiency analysis (model size and FPS) shows the method remains competitive or better than several baselines, addressing practical deployment concerns.

The paper is clearly written, well-illustrated with architecture diagrams (Figs. 2-4), and provides sufficient mathematical formalization of the rendering and loss functions for both NeRF and 3DGS pipelines.
weaknesses: The core idea (using self-supervised DINO features as auxiliary supervision) is conceptually incremental; the novelty largely resides in the specific attention-based fusion module (SSE), whose design choices (e.g., two-stage cross-attention between geometry, appearance, and DINO features) are not ablated or theoretically motivated beyond empirical results.

Several reported improvements in the generality study (Table 4) are marginal (e.g., completion unchanged for Co-SLAM, small PSNR/SSIM gains for SplaTAM/MonoGS), and no variance or repeated-run statistics are provided to assess significance.

No visualization or analysis explicitly demonstrating the claimed 'hierarchical scene understanding' or 'part-whole relationships' captured by EDINO features (e.g., feature-space t-SNE, attention maps), leaving this central claim only indirectly supported by downstream metrics.

Runtime/memory analysis does not clarify whether the cost of DINO feature extraction (ViT-small) and SSE inference is included in the reported FPS, which is important given DINO backbones are typically non-trivial in compute cost for real-time SLAM claims.

Limitations and failure-case discussion are minimal (a single sentence on future work), with no analysis of when/why DINO-based cues might fail (e.g., texture-less DINO ambiguity, dynamic scenes, or scenes dissimilar to DINO's training distribution).

Some baseline numbers appear to be taken directly from original papers rather than re-evaluated under an identical protocol (e.g., PLGSLAM marked with †), which could introduce inconsistencies in comparison fairness.

No code/release statement is provided, and several implementation details (e.g., full hyperparameter settings for SSE, training schedules) are only partially specified, which may hinder reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated idea: leveraging self-supervised DINO features to inject higher-level, continuous scene structure information into radiance-field-based SLAM systems, avoiding the need for semantic annotations required by prior semantic SLAM approaches.

The proposed Scene Structure Encoder (SSE) with cross-attention between geometric and appearance-refined DINO features to produce EDINO is a reasonably novel architectural contribution, and the ablations (Table 5) convincingly show that EDINO outperforms using raw DINO features alone, justifying the added complexity.

Strong demonstration of generality: the method is plugged into five different underlying SLAM architectures (hash-grid, tri-plane, neural-point, and two 3DGS variants), with consistent improvements shown in Table 4, supporting the claim of broad applicability rather than being tied to one specific baseline.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) with tracking, reconstruction, and rendering quality metrics, plus runtime/memory analysis (Table 6) showing the method is not substantially heavier than baselines despite added feature branches.
Clear method exposition with detailed equations and figures for both the NeRF-based and 3DGS-based pipelines, aiding reproducibility of the core technical ideas.
weaknesses: The performance gains over the strongest baselines are often marginal and inconsistent across metrics (e.g., Table 1 NeRF results: DINO-SLAM is worse in Acc. and Depth L1 than Point-SLAM/PLGSLAM; Table 2 ScanNet: DINO-SLAM(3DGS) ATE is worse than SplaTAM on scene 0000), which somewhat undercuts the 'superior performance' framing given the added architectural complexity.

No computational/training cost analysis for the SSE itself (e.g., additional training time to learn EDINO features, or whether DINO/SSE inference is amortized online vs. precomputed), and Table 6 does not clearly disentangle SSE overhead from the base pipeline runtime.

The paper does not discuss failure cases or limitations of using self-supervised DINO features (e.g., in textureless, repetitive, or highly dynamic scenes) which would be relevant given the paper's motivation around scene understanding; a brief limitations discussion is absent.

The SSE architecture, while reasonable, is a fairly standard cross-attention refinement module applied to features from an existing pretrained model (DINO); the core novelty is somewhat incremental relative to substantial prior work combining semantic/feature priors with SLAM (e.g., SNI-SLAM is used as a baseline but SSE's technical distinctiveness relative to such feature-fusion designs is not deeply analyzed).

No qualitative visualization of the EDINO/DINO feature maps themselves is provided to give intuition about what structural information the SSE is actually capturing beyond aggregate downstream metrics.

strengths: Broad and thorough empirical validation across 7 different scene representations (hash-grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, 2D Gaussian surfels) and multiple SLAM baselines, demonstrating the generality of the proposed SGE module rather than a single cherry-picked integration.

Consistent improvements are shown on three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM), covering tracking accuracy, reconstruction quality, and novel-view rendering, with the method achieving state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art results in most settings.

The ablation in Table 2 (vanilla DINO vs. concat(DINO,depth) vs. geoDINO) is a well-designed experiment that isolates the actual contribution of the geometry-aware attention mechanism versus a naive depth-concatenation baseline, providing good evidence that the SGE design choice matters, not just the addition of any geometric signal.

The paper includes practical analyses beyond raw accuracy: runtime/FPS overhead, memory footprint, and robustness to depth noise, which are useful for assessing real-world applicability of the approach.

The method is conceptually simple (attention-based fusion of DINO features and depth-derived geometric features) and clearly described, making it plausible to reproduce and integrate into other SLAM pipelines as claimed.
weaknesses: The magnitude of improvements is often small and sometimes inconsistent (e.g., Fig. 1 shows the proposed method underperforming SOTA on some PSNR/completion entries: 39.04 vs 38.04, 44.19 vs 38.04, 44.6 vs 41.22), which slightly undercuts the "superior performance" framing in the abstract/intro; the paper would benefit from more careful, consistent claims tied to the actual per-scene variability.

No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported for any table, making it hard to judge whether the reported gains (often 0.5-2 points on RMSE or PSNR) are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run noise inherent to SLAM systems.

The additional supervision losses (Lgf, LDf) and geoDINO features add non-trivial training-time cost (extra forward/backward passes, larger memory footprint as in Table 7-8) without an accompanying analysis of cost-benefit trade-off relative to simpler, cheaper geometry-aware baselines (e.g., using depth-conditioned convolutional features instead of full cross-attention).

The description of how the SGE feature is used at inference/rendering time versus training time is not fully detailed (e.ger, whether the SGE runs online for every frame or is used only during optimization, and how features generalize to unseen viewpoints), leaving some reproducibility gaps.

The related-work discussion of prior DINO-informed SLAM works [37,40,56,61,62] is fairly brief and could more clearly delineate the technical novelty of the cross-attention SGE architecture relative to these very closely related efforts, several of which already combine DINO/DINOv2 with SLAM.

The paper claims wide applicability to "future NeRF/GS SLAM systems," but all experiments use RGB-D input with known depth; the robustness-to-depth-noise experiment is limited to a single Gaussian noise level on one scene, which is a fairly weak test of real-world sensor noise conditions (e.g., structured noise, missing depth, low-cost sensor artifacts).

strengths: The proposed Scene Geometry Encoder (SGE) is validated across an unusually wide range of scene representations (hash-grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, 2D Gaussian surfels), and Table 1 shows consistent improvements when plugged into seven different existing SLAM baselines, supporting the claim of general applicability.

The ablation in Table 2 is well designed: it isolates the contribution of vanilla DINO features, a naive depth-concatenation baseline, and the proposed geoDINO features, convincingly showing that geometry-aware lifting of DINO features is responsible for most of the gain rather than the mere presence of semantic features.

The method achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive tracking and mapping/rendering accuracy on three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) for both NeRF-based and GS-based pipelines, which is a fairly comprehensive empirical validation.

The paper includes a reasonably thorough analysis of computational overhead (FPS, memory footprint, per-module runtime breakdown) and a robustness-to-depth-noise experiment, which add useful practical context beyond raw accuracy numbers.
The paper is clearly written and the architecture (Figures 2-5) is well illustrated, making the pipeline easy to follow and facilitating potential reproduction.
weaknesses: Although the motivation repeatedly emphasizes higher-level 'semantic understanding' enabled by DINO, no experiment directly evaluates semantic quality (e.g., segmentation, open-vocabulary retrieval) of the learned geoDINO features; all reported metrics are purely photometric/geometric (PSNR, RMSE, accuracy/completion), leaving the central semantic claim largely unverified.

The SGE architecture (two-stage cross-attention between projected DINO and depth features) is a fairly standard fusion module; the technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the empirical/engineering contribution.

The claimed 'negligible overhead' is inconsistent with the reported FPS drop for the NeRF-based pipeline (ESLAM 4.62 -> DINO-SLAM 2.55 FPS, ~45% reduction), which is a non-trivial cost for a real-time SLAM system and deserves more discussion.

State-of-the-art claims are somewhat overstated: several tables show other methods outperforming DINO-SLAM on individual scenes/metrics (e.g., PLGSLAM's average RMSE on ScanNet, MonoGS on TUM fr1_desk), and this is not always clearly acknowledged in the text.

Generality/ablation experiments (Tables 1-2) are conducted only on Replica; it would strengthen the paper to show the same component-wise ablation on ScanNet or TUM, which contain more challenging real-world imperfect depth and longer trajectories.

No discussion of failure cases (e.g., dynamic objects, textureless regions, or scenes where geometry cues from depth are unreliable beyond the single synthetic noise experiment) or of code/data release for reproducibility.
